decks.title: Polynomials — Part 1: Zeroes and their graphs
goals: Find the zero of a linear polynomial and test whether a number is a zero
Read the number of zeroes and their values from the graph of y = p(x)
Describe the shapes of graphs of linear, quadratic and cubic polynomials
Interpret zeroes in real situations and reject meaningless ones

slides.heading: Polynomials, Part 1: Zeroes and their graphs
slides.body_md: Where a graph meets the $x$-axis, the polynomial is zero.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x squared minus 2 x minus 3, an upward parabola crossing the x-axis at minus 1 and 3, marked as the two zeroes.
visual.caption: The zeroes $-1$ and $3$ are where the graph meets the $x$-axis.

slides.narration: Welcome to Polynomials, part one. On the screen is a curve called a parabola. It dips below the horizontal axis and comes back up, meeting the axis at exactly two points. Those two crossing points hide the most important numbers of the polynomial, called its zeroes. Today you will learn to find zeroes from a graph and see why the graph tells you how many there can be.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Read zeroes from the graph of $y = p(x)$
Know the shapes: line, parabola, cubic curve
slides.narration: These are your goals for this part. The big idea links algebra and pictures: a zero is a number that makes the polynomial equal to zero, and on the graph it is a crossing point with the horizontal axis. Keep that one sentence in mind and every question in this part becomes easier.

slides.heading: Polynomials and degree
slides.body_md: A **polynomial** in $x$ has only whole-number powers of $x$. Its **degree** is the highest power.

visual.alt: Table: 3 x minus 7 is linear with degree 1; 2 x squared minus x plus 5 is quadratic with degree 2; x cubed minus 4 x is cubic with degree 3; x squared plus 1 over x and root x plus 1 are not polynomials because of negative or fractional powers.
visual.caption: Degree $1$: linear. Degree $2$: quadratic. Degree $3$: cubic.

slides.narration: A polynomial allows only powers like zero, one, two, three of x, multiplied by numbers and added up. One over x is x to the power minus one, and the square root of x is x to the power half, so expressions with them are not polynomials. The highest power is the degree, and it names the polynomial: linear, quadratic or cubic.

slides.heading: Value of a polynomial and its zeroes
slides.body_md: Put a number in place of $x$ to get the **value** $p(k)$. If $p(k) = 0$, then $k$ is a **zero** of $p(x)$.

visual.alt: Table of values of p of x equals x squared minus 5 x plus 6 for x from 0 to 4: the values are 6, 2, 0, 0, 2, so 2 and 3 are zeroes.
visual.caption: $p(2) = 0$ and $p(3) = 0$: the zeroes are $2$ and $3$.

slides.narration: To find a value, substitute and calculate. For x squared minus five x plus six, putting in two gives four minus ten plus six, which is zero. So two is a zero. Three works too. Notice the values go down to zero and come back up. That pattern is exactly the parabola shape we will see on the graph.

slides.heading: Linear polynomials: one zero
slides.body_md: The graph of $ax + b$ ($a \ne 0$) is a straight line. It meets the $x$-axis exactly once, at $x = -\dfrac ba$.

visual.alt: Graph of the straight line y equals 2 x minus 4, crossing the x-axis at 2, its only zero, and the y-axis at minus 4.
visual.caption: A linear polynomial $ax + b$ has exactly one zero, $-\dfrac ba$.

slides.narration: A linear polynomial draws a straight line that is not flat, so it must cross the horizontal axis exactly once. Solve two x minus four equals zero to get two, and that is exactly where the line crosses. In general the zero of a x plus b is minus b over a. Watch the sign: it is minus b, divided by a.

slides.heading: Quick check: a linear zero
slides.body_md: Find the zero of a linear polynomial.
slides.narration: Set the polynomial equal to zero and solve. Be careful with the sign when you move the constant across, and with which number goes on top of the fraction.

slides.heading: Quadratics: parabolas up or down
slides.body_md: The graph of $ax^2 + bx + c$ ($a \ne 0$) is a **parabola**. It opens **upward** if $a > 0$ and **downward** if $a < 0$.

visual.alt: Two parabolas: y equals x squared minus 4 opens upward and crosses the x-axis at minus 2 and 2; y equals minus x squared plus 2 x plus 3 opens downward and crosses the x-axis at minus 1 and 3.
visual.caption: Up if $a > 0$, down if $a < 0$.

slides.narration: Every quadratic draws a parabola. The sign of the number in front of x squared decides the direction. Positive, and the arms point up like a cup. Negative, and the arms point down like a cap, as in the path of a thrown ball. Both parabolas here cross the axis twice, so each has two zeroes.

slides.heading: Two, one or no zeroes
slides.body_md: A parabola can cross the $x$-axis twice, **touch** it once, or miss it completely.

visual.alt: Three upward parabolas with the same shape stacked one unit apart: y equals x squared minus 4 x plus 3 crosses the x-axis at 1 and 3; y equals x squared minus 4 x plus 4 touches it at 2; y equals x squared minus 4 x plus 5 stays above it and has no zeroes.
visual.caption: A quadratic has two, one or no zeroes.

slides.narration: Here the same parabola is lifted one step at a time. At first it crosses the axis twice. Lift it by one and it just touches the axis at two: one zero. Lift it again and it floats above the axis: no zeroes at all. So a quadratic has at most two zeroes, and sometimes fewer.

slides.heading: Degree limits the number of zeroes
slides.body_md: A polynomial of degree $n$ has **at most** $n$ zeroes: its graph meets the $x$-axis at most $n$ times.

visual.alt: Table: a degree 1 polynomial has a straight-line graph and exactly one zero; degree 2 has a parabola and 0, 1 or 2 zeroes; degree 3 has a cubic curve and 1, 2 or 3 zeroes.
visual.caption: Never more zeroes than the degree.

slides.narration: This rule is worth remembering word for word: a polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes. A line has exactly one, a quadratic up to two, a cubic up to three. A cubic always has at least one, because its two ends go in opposite directions, one up and one down, so it must cross the axis somewhere.

slides.heading: Graphs of cubic polynomials
slides.body_md: A cubic curve can cross the $x$-axis three times, cross once, or cross once and touch once.

visual.alt: Three cubic curves: x cubed minus 4 x crosses the x-axis at minus 2, 0 and 2; x cubed crosses only at 0; x cubed minus 3 x plus 2 crosses at minus 2 and touches at 1.
visual.caption: A cubic has one, two or three zeroes — never more than three.

slides.narration: Here are three cubics. The first crosses three times, at minus two, zero and two. The plain x cubed crosses only once, at the origin. The third crosses at minus two and just touches at one. In every case, count the points where the curve meets the axis; that count is the number of zeroes. You do not need the formula of the curve to count them.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: zeroes from a graph
slides.body_md: The graph of $y = p(x)$ is shown. Find the number of zeroes and the zeroes. What is the least possible degree of $p(x)$?
bullets: **Step 1 —** Look only at where the curve meets the $x$-axis.
**Step 2 —** It meets the axis at $x = -2, -1, 1, 2$: **four** zeroes.
**Step 3 —** A polynomial with four zeroes has degree at least $4$.

visual.alt: A W-shaped curve, the graph of x to the fourth minus 5 x squared plus 4, crossing the x-axis at minus 2, minus 1, 1 and 2.
visual.caption: Four crossings, so four zeroes.

slides.narration: Ignore the bumps and the y-axis; focus on the horizontal axis. The curve meets it four times, so there are four zeroes, and their values are the x-coordinates: minus two, minus one, one and two. Because a polynomial cannot have more zeroes than its degree, this one must have degree four or more. The factorised form confirms the reading.

slides.heading: Quick check: count from the graph
slides.body_md: Use the graph to count the zeroes.
slides.narration: Count the points where the curve meets the horizontal axis, not the turning points. A point exactly at the origin still counts as a zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: when does the ball land?
slides.body_md: From a rooftop in Pune, a ball is thrown upward. Its height after $t$ seconds is $h = -5t^2 + 10t + 15$ metres. When does it reach the ground?
bullets: **Step 3 —** Time cannot be negative: reject $t = -1$. The ball lands after $3$ s.

visual.alt: Graph of the height h equals minus 5 t squared plus 10 t plus 15 against time t: a downward parabola starting at 15 metres at t equals 0, rising to 20 metres at t equals 1, and reaching the ground at t equals 3. The other zero, t equals minus 1, is marked as rejected.
visual.caption: Only the zero $t = 3$ makes sense: time cannot be negative.

slides.narration: In a real situation, a zero has a meaning. Here the height is zero when the ball hits the ground. The algebra gives two zeroes, three and minus one, but minus one second is before the throw happened, so we reject it. The graph agrees: the curve starts at fifteen metres, rises to twenty, and lands at three seconds.

slides.heading: Intercepts: zeroes and the constant term
slides.body_md: Zeroes are the **$x$-intercepts**. The **$y$-intercept** is $p(0)$, which equals the constant term $c$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals 2 x squared plus x minus 6, crossing the x-axis at minus 2 and 1.5 and the y-axis at minus 6.
visual.caption: Zeroes on the $x$-axis; $p(0) = c$ on the $y$-axis.

slides.narration: Two different intercepts, two different meanings. Where the curve crosses the horizontal axis, you read the zeroes, here minus two and one point five. Where it crosses the vertical axis, you read p of zero, which is always just the constant term, here minus six. Students often mix these up, so say aloud which axis you are reading.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false
slides.body_md: Decide whether the statement about degree and zeroes is true.
slides.narration: Think of the graph. How many times can a curve of degree n meet the horizontal axis? Picture a parabola and try to make it cross three times.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: On the graph: zeroes are where $y = p(x)$ meets the $x$-axis
Linear: one zero $-\dfrac ba$. Quadratic: parabola, $0$, $1$ or $2$ zeroes
In context, reject zeroes that make no sense

visual.alt: Summary table listing a linear polynomial with one zero, three quadratics with two, one and no zeroes, and a cubic with three zeroes, alongside the shape of each graph.
visual.caption: Count the meeting points with the $x$-axis.

slides.narration: To sum up: a zero makes the polynomial zero, and on the graph it is a meeting point with the horizontal axis. Lines have one zero, parabolas up to two, cubic curves up to three, and in general a degree n polynomial has at most n. In a real problem, keep only the zeroes that make sense.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Graph-reading MCQ (1 mark):** count meeting points with the $x$-axis — touching counts once
**Draw-the-graph questions:** table of values 1 + plotting and smooth curve 1 + zeroes read correctly 1
**Mistake:** counting turning points instead of axis crossings
**Mistake:** writing zeroes with the signs of the factors, e.g. $(x + 2)(x - 5)$ → "$2, -5$"
**Mistake:** keeping a negative time or length as an answer
slides.narration: Graph questions are quick marks if you stay disciplined. Count only the points on the horizontal axis. A parabola that just touches the axis gives one zero, not two. When a question gives factors such as x plus two, the zero is minus two, so flip the sign. And in word problems, examiners give a mark for rejecting the answer that does not make sense.

decks.title: Polynomials — Part 2: Zeroes and coefficients of a quadratic
goals: Find the zeroes of a quadratic polynomial by splitting the middle term
Verify that the sum of zeroes is −b/a and the product is c/a
Form a quadratic polynomial from the sum and product of its zeroes
Find unknown coefficients from given conditions on the zeroes
Evaluate symmetric expressions such as α² + β² without finding the zeroes

slides.heading: Polynomials, Part 2: Zeroes and coefficients
slides.body_md: The coefficients already know the sum and product of the zeroes.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x squared minus 7 x plus 10, an upward parabola crossing the x-axis at 2 and 5.
visual.caption: Zeroes $2$ and $5$: sum $7$, product $10$ — read straight from the coefficients.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Look at x squared minus seven x plus ten. Its zeroes are two and five. Add them and you get seven; multiply them and you get ten. Both numbers are sitting in the polynomial itself. That is not a coincidence, and in this lesson you will see why it always happens and how examiners use it.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find zeroes by **splitting the middle term**
Build a quadratic from a given sum and product
Find unknown coefficients from conditions on zeroes
slides.narration: These are the goals. The second one is the heart of the chapter, and almost every board question on this topic uses it, either forwards, from polynomial to zeroes, or backwards, from zeroes to polynomial. We will use the Greek letters alpha and beta for the two zeroes.

slides.heading: Splitting the middle term
slides.body_md: For $ax^2 + bx + c$, find two numbers whose **product is $ac$** and whose **sum is $b$**. Split $bx$ with them and factorise in pairs.

visual.alt: Table of three quadratics factorised by splitting the middle term: x squared minus 7 x plus 10 into x minus 2 times x minus 5 with zeroes 2 and 5; 2 x squared plus x minus 6 into 2 x minus 3 times x plus 2 with zeroes 3 over 2 and minus 2; 10 x squared minus 3 x minus 1 into 2 x minus 1 times 5 x plus 1 with zeroes one half and minus one fifth.
visual.caption: Each factor $(px + q)$ gives the zero $-\dfrac qp$.

slides.narration: To find zeroes by algebra, factorise. Multiply the first and last coefficients, then hunt for two numbers with that product and with the middle coefficient as their sum. Split the middle term with them and group in pairs. Each bracket gives one zero: set it equal to zero and solve. Signs matter, so check your two numbers before splitting.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: zeroes and the relationship
slides.body_md: Find the zeroes of $10x^2 - 3x - 1$ and verify the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals 10 x squared minus 3 x minus 1, crossing the x-axis at minus 0.2 and 0.5.
visual.caption: Zeroes $-\dfrac15$ and $\dfrac12$.

slides.narration: This is the classic two or three mark question. First factorise carefully. Then write the zeroes as fractions. Finally compute the sum and product from the zeroes, and separately from the coefficients, and show they match. Write both sides each time: the examiner wants to see the verification, not just the answer.

slides.heading: Why sum $= -\dfrac ba$ and product $= \dfrac ca$
slides.body_md: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the zeroes, then $ax^2 + bx + c = a(x - \alpha)(x - \beta)$. Expand and compare coefficients.

visual.alt: Table comparing coefficients: the x squared terms match as a; the x term b equals minus a times the sum of zeroes; the constant c equals a times the product of zeroes.
visual.caption: Matching coefficients gives both relationships.

slides.narration: Here is why it works. A quadratic with zeroes alpha and beta must be a times x minus alpha times x minus beta. Expand it and line up the terms. The x term says b equals minus a times the sum, and the constant says c equals a times the product. Divide by a and you have both rules. Notice the minus sign belongs to the sum only.

slides.heading: The relationship in action
slides.body_md: Sum and product can be read **without** finding the zeroes.

visual.alt: Table verifying the relationships for three quadratics: x squared minus 7 x plus 10 has sum 7 and product 10; 2 x squared plus x minus 6 has sum minus one half and product minus 3; 4 x squared minus 9 has sum 0 and product minus nine quarters, each matching minus b over a and c over a.
visual.caption: When $b = 0$ the zeroes are opposites and their sum is $0$.

slides.narration: Read across each row: the sum and product from the zeroes always match the values from the coefficients. Look at the last row. There is no x term, so b is zero, and the zeroes are a number and its negative, which add to zero. This is a quick way to answer one mark questions without factorising at all.

slides.heading: Quick check: sum of zeroes
slides.body_md: Find the sum of the zeroes straight from the coefficients.
slides.narration: Identify a and b, with their signs. The rule has a minus sign in front; that is where most marks are lost.

slides.heading: Forming a quadratic from its zeroes
slides.body_md: If the sum of zeroes is $S$ and the product is $P$, a quadratic with these zeroes is
bullets: Any non-zero $k$ gives the same zeroes: there are infinitely many such polynomials
Choose $k$ to clear fractions, e.g. $k = $ the common denominator

visual.alt: Table forming polynomials from sum and product: sum 5 and product 6 give x squared minus 5 x plus 6; sum minus three halves and product minus 1 give 2 x squared plus 3 x minus 2; sum 0 and product minus 5 give x squared minus 5.
visual.caption: Minus the sum, plus the product.

slides.narration: Going backwards is just as easy. Write x squared, minus the sum times x, plus the product. Remember: minus sum, plus product. Then multiply by any non-zero number you like, usually to clear fractions. Questions say a quadratic polynomial, not the quadratic polynomial, because there are infinitely many with the same zeroes.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: from sum and product
slides.body_md: Find a quadratic polynomial whose zeroes have sum $-\dfrac32$ and product $-1$. Then find its zeroes.

visual.alt: Three parabolas of the form k times 2 x squared plus 3 x minus 2, for k equal to 1, minus 1 and one half. They have different shapes and directions but all cross the x-axis at the same two points, minus 2 and 0.5.
visual.caption: Same zeroes, different $k$: infinitely many quadratics share a pair of zeroes.

slides.narration: Substitute the sum and product into minus sum, plus product. A negative sum becomes a plus sign, so be careful. Then multiply by two to clear the fraction. The graph shows something important: multiplying by different values of k changes the shape, even flips it, but every curve still passes through the same two zeroes.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: irrational zeroes
slides.body_md: Find a quadratic polynomial whose zeroes are $3 + \sqrt2$ and $3 - \sqrt2$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x squared minus 6 x plus 7, crossing the x-axis at 3 minus root 2, about 1.59, and 3 plus root 2, about 4.41, symmetric about x equals 3.
visual.caption: Irrational zeroes still have a rational sum ($6$) and product ($7$).

slides.narration: Zeroes do not have to be whole numbers. These two are irrational, but they come as a pair, three plus root two and three minus root two, so the roots cancel in the sum and in the product. You get a polynomial with whole-number coefficients. The graph crosses at about one point six and four point four, balanced around three.

slides.heading: Quick check: find the missing coefficient
slides.body_md: One zero is given. Find the unknown coefficient.
slides.narration: If a number is a zero, substituting it makes the polynomial equal to zero. Substitute, then solve the simple equation for k.

slides.heading: Symmetric expressions in α and β
slides.body_md: Expressions that do not change when $\alpha$ and $\beta$ swap can be written using $\alpha + \beta$ and $\alpha\beta$ only.

headers: In terms of sum and product

visual.alt: Table of symmetric expressions: alpha squared plus beta squared equals sum squared minus twice the product; one over alpha plus one over beta equals sum over product; alpha minus beta, squared, equals sum squared minus four times the product; alpha squared beta plus alpha beta squared equals product times sum; alpha cubed plus beta cubed equals sum cubed minus three times product times sum.
visual.caption: Learn the first three by heart.

slides.narration: Sometimes the zeroes are messy, but a question asks for something like alpha squared plus beta squared. Do not find the zeroes. Use an identity to rewrite the expression with the sum and product, which you can read from the coefficients. The first identity is the most common: the square of the sum, minus twice the product.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a garden without the sides
slides.body_md: The length and breadth (in m) of a rectangular garden in Pune are the zeroes of $x^2 - 17x + 60$. Find its perimeter, area and diagonal **without** finding the sides.
bullets: **Step 2 —** Perimeter $= 2(l + b) = 34$ m; area $= lb = 60$ m².
**Step 3 —** Diagonal$^2 = l^2 + b^2 = 17^2 - 2 \times 60 = 289 - 120 = 169$, so the diagonal is $13$ m.

visual.alt: Rectangle ABCD, 12 metres by 5 metres, with the dashed diagonal AC of 13 metres.
visual.caption: Sides are the zeroes of $x^2 - 17x + 60$; diagonal$^2 = 17^2 - 2 \times 60 = 169$.

slides.narration: This is where symmetric expressions shine. Perimeter needs the sum, area needs the product, and the diagonal needs the sum of squares, which is the sum squared minus twice the product. Thirteen metres, without ever finding the sides. The check confirms it: the sides are twelve and five, a famous right triangle.

slides.heading: Quick check: assertion and reason
slides.body_md: Test the assertion with the rule in the reason.
slides.narration: Work out the sum of the zeroes using the rule with its minus sign. Then compare it with the value in the assertion, sign and all.

slides.heading: Which way are you going?
slides.body_md: Decide the direction first; then the method is automatic.

nodes.label: Zeroes, or their sum and product
Need the zeroes? Factorise (split the middle term)
Need a symmetric expression? Use sum $-\dfrac ba$ and product $\dfrac ca$
Unknown coefficient? Substitute a zero, or use a sum/product condition

visual.alt: Decision chart: if a polynomial is given, factorise to get the zeroes, use minus b over a and c over a for symmetric expressions, or substitute a known zero to find an unknown coefficient; if the zeroes or their sum and product are given, write k times x squared minus S x plus P and clear fractions.
visual.caption: Forwards: polynomial → zeroes. Backwards: zeroes → polynomial.

slides.narration: Before you write anything, ask which way the question is going. From polynomial to zeroes, you factorise, or use the sum and product rules if you only need a symmetric expression. From zeroes to polynomial, you write minus sum, plus product. If a coefficient is unknown, substitute a known zero or turn the condition into an equation.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Splitting the middle term: two numbers with product $ac$ and sum $b$
A known zero makes $p(\text{zero}) = 0$: use it to find a coefficient

visual.alt: Summary table: from a polynomial use minus b over a and c over a; from a sum and product write k times x squared minus S x plus P; from a known zero substitute to find a coefficient, each with an example.
visual.caption: Three directions, three tools.

slides.narration: Here is the whole part in a few lines. Factorise by splitting the middle term. The sum of zeroes is minus b over a and the product is c over a. To build a polynomial, use minus sum, plus product, times any non-zero k. For harder expressions, rewrite them with the sum and product. And a known zero always gives you an equation.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Find zeroes and verify (2–3 marks):** factorisation 1 + zeroes 1 + both relations shown 1
**Form a polynomial (2 marks):** sum and product 1 + polynomial 1 (any non-zero multiple is accepted)
**Mistake:** sum $= \dfrac ba$ — the minus sign is missing
**Mistake:** $x^2 + Sx + P$ instead of $x^2 - Sx + P$
**Not in syllabus:** sum/product relations for cubics, and the division algorithm
slides.narration: In verification questions, write both sides for the sum and both sides for the product; a bare tick earns nothing. When forming a polynomial, any non-zero multiple gets full marks, so clear fractions freely. The three classic slips are the missing minus in minus b over a, plus instead of minus before the sum, and forgetting the minus two alpha beta.

notes.title: Polynomials — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Polynomials and degree
sections.body_md:
A **polynomial** in $x$ is a sum of terms $ax^n$ where $n$ is a whole number ($0, 1, 2, \dots$). The highest power with a non-zero coefficient is the **degree**.

- Degree $1$: **linear**, $ax + b$ ($a \ne 0$).
- Degree $2$: **quadratic**, $ax^2 + bx + c$ ($a \ne 0$).
- Degree $3$: **cubic**, $ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$ ($a \ne 0$).

$x^2 + \dfrac1x$ and $\sqrt x + 1$ are **not** polynomials (powers $-1$ and $\dfrac12$).

key_terms.definition_md: An expression made of terms $ax^n$ with whole-number powers $n$.
The highest power of the variable with a non-zero coefficient.

visual.alt: Table of four expressions with their degree and type: linear, quadratic, cubic, and root x plus 1, which is not a polynomial.
visual.caption: Degree names the polynomial.

sections.heading: 2. Value and zeroes of a polynomial
sections.body_md:
The **value** of $p(x)$ at $x = k$ is $p(k)$, found by substitution. A real number $k$ is a **zero** of $p(x)$ if $p(k) = 0$.

The zero of a linear polynomial $ax + b$ is $-\dfrac ba$.

To **test** a zero, substitute: $p(x) = x^2 - 3x + 2$ gives $p(2) = 4 - 6 + 2 = 0$, so $2$ is a zero. A known zero gives an equation for an unknown coefficient: if $3$ is a zero of $x^2 + kx + 15$, then $9 + 3k + 15 = 0$ and $k = -8$.

visual.alt: Table of values of x squared minus 5 x plus 6 at x equals 0 to 4, giving 6, 2, 0, 0 and 2, so 2 and 3 are zeroes.
visual.caption: Values of $p(x)$: the zeroes are $2$ and $3$.

sections.heading: 3. Geometrical meaning of the zeroes
sections.body_md:
The zeroes of $p(x)$ are the **$x$-coordinates of the points where the graph of $y = p(x)$ meets the $x$-axis**.

- **Linear:** a straight line, exactly one zero.
- **Quadratic:** a **parabola**, opening upward if $a > 0$ and downward if $a < 0$. It can cross the $x$-axis twice (two zeroes), touch it once (one zero), or not meet it (no zero).
- The $y$-intercept is $p(0)$, the constant term — not a zero.

key_terms.definition_md: The U-shaped graph of a quadratic polynomial.
A point where a graph meets the $x$-axis; its $x$-coordinate is a zero.

visual.alt: Three upward parabolas with the same shape stacked one unit apart: y equals x squared minus 4 x plus 3 crosses the x-axis at 1 and 3; y equals x squared minus 4 x plus 4 touches it at 2; y equals x squared minus 4 x plus 5 stays above it and has no zeroes.
visual.caption: A quadratic has two, one or no zeroes.

visuals.alt: Two parabolas: y equals x squared minus 4 opens upward and crosses the x-axis at minus 2 and 2; y equals minus x squared plus 2 x plus 3 opens downward and crosses the x-axis at minus 1 and 3.
visuals.caption: Up if $a > 0$, down if $a < 0$.

sections.heading: 4. Number of zeroes and higher degrees
sections.body_md:
A polynomial of degree $n$ has **at most $n$ zeroes**, because its graph meets the $x$-axis at most $n$ times.

- Cubic: $1$, $2$ or $3$ zeroes (at least one, because its two ends go in opposite directions).
- The graph of $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4$ meets the axis at $\pm1$ and $\pm2$: four zeroes.

To count zeroes from a graph, count the meeting points with the $x$-axis — not the turning points, and not the $y$-intercept.

**In context**, keep only meaningful zeroes: for $h = -5t^2 + 10t + 15$ the zeroes are $-1$ and $3$, and the ball lands at $t = 3$ s.

key_terms.definition_md: The graph of a degree-3 polynomial; it meets the $x$-axis one, two or three times.

visual.alt: Three cubic curves: x cubed minus 4 x crosses the x-axis at minus 2, 0 and 2; x cubed crosses only at 0; x cubed minus 3 x plus 2 crosses at minus 2 and touches at 1.
visual.caption: A cubic has one, two or three zeroes — never more than three.

visuals.alt: Graph of the height h equals minus 5 t squared plus 10 t plus 15 against time t: a downward parabola starting at 15 metres at t equals 0, rising to 20 metres at t equals 1, and reaching the ground at t equals 3. The other zero, t equals minus 1, is marked as rejected.
visuals.caption: Only the zero $t = 3$ makes sense: time cannot be negative.

sections.heading: 5. Finding zeroes by splitting the middle term
sections.body_md:
To factorise $ax^2 + bx + c$: find two numbers with **product $ac$** and **sum $b$**, split $bx$ into two terms with them, and factorise in pairs.

Example: $10x^2 - 3x - 1$: $ac = -10 = (-5)(2)$, $-5 + 2 = -3$. So $10x^2 - 5x + 2x - 1 = (5x + 1)(2x - 1)$, zeroes $-\dfrac15$ and $\dfrac12$.

Each factor $(px + q)$ gives the zero $-\dfrac qp$. Difference of squares: $9t^2 - 16 = (3t - 4)(3t + 4)$.

key_terms.definition_md: Writing $bx$ as a sum of two terms whose coefficients multiply to $ac$, then factorising in pairs.

sections.heading: 6. Relationship between zeroes and coefficients
sections.body_md:
If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the zeroes of $ax^2 + bx + c$ ($a \ne 0$), then

$$\alpha + \beta = -\dfrac ba, \qquad \alpha\beta = \dfrac ca.$$

**Why:** $ax^2 + bx + c = a(x - \alpha)(x - \beta) = ax^2 - a(\alpha + \beta)x + a\alpha\beta$; compare coefficients.

Use it to **verify** factorisations, to read the sum and product without factorising, and to find unknown coefficients from conditions (reciprocal zeroes ⇒ product $1$; opposite zeroes ⇒ sum $0$).

*Not in the 2026–27 syllabus:* the relationship for cubic polynomials, and the division algorithm.

visual.caption: Sum and product straight from the coefficients.

sections.heading: 7. Forming a quadratic polynomial
sections.body_md:
If the sum of the zeroes is $S$ and the product is $P$, then every quadratic with these zeroes is

$$k(x^2 - Sx + P), \quad k \ne 0.$$

Choose $k$ to clear fractions. Examples: zeroes $-3, 4$ → $x^2 - x - 12$; sum $-\dfrac32$, product $-1$ → $2x^2 + 3x - 2$; zeroes $3 \pm \sqrt2$ → $x^2 - 6x + 7$.

New zeroes from old: if $\alpha, \beta$ are zeroes of $x^2 - 7x + 10$, the polynomial with zeroes $\alpha^2, \beta^2$ has sum $\alpha^2 + \beta^2 = 29$ and product $(\alpha\beta)^2 = 100$: $x^2 - 29x + 100$.

key_terms.definition_md: All polynomials $k(x^2 - Sx + P)$, $k \ne 0$, which share the same zeroes.

sections.heading: 8. Symmetric expressions in the zeroes
sections.body_md:
Expressions unchanged by swapping $\alpha$ and $\beta$ can be evaluated from the sum and product, without finding the zeroes:

- $\alpha^2 + \beta^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 2\alpha\beta$
- $\dfrac1\alpha + \dfrac1\beta = \dfrac{\alpha + \beta}{\alpha\beta}$
- $(\alpha - \beta)^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 4\alpha\beta$
- $\alpha^2\beta + \alpha\beta^2 = \alpha\beta(\alpha + \beta)$
- $\alpha^3 + \beta^3 = (\alpha + \beta)^3 - 3\alpha\beta(\alpha + \beta)$

**Application:** sides of a rectangle as zeroes of $x^2 - 17x + 60$: perimeter $34$ m, area $60$ m², diagonal $\sqrt{17^2 - 120} = 13$ m.

key_terms.definition_md: An expression in $\alpha$ and $\beta$ that does not change when they are swapped.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Find zeroes and verify the relationship (2–3 marks):* factorisation 1, zeroes 1, sum and product each checked against $-\dfrac ba$ and $\dfrac ca$ 1.
- *Form a quadratic polynomial (2 marks):* sum and product 1, polynomial 1 — any non-zero multiple is accepted.
- *Graph questions:* table of values, smooth curve, zeroes read from the $x$-axis.
- *Symmetric expressions (2–5 marks):* identity 1, substitution 1, answer 1 per part.

**Common mistakes**
1. Sum of zeroes written as $\dfrac ba$ (missing minus).
2. Polynomial written as $x^2 + Sx + P$.
3. $\alpha^2 + \beta^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2$, forgetting $-2\alpha\beta$.
4. Reading the $y$-intercept as a zero, or counting turning points as zeroes.
5. Zero of $(x + 2)$ written as $2$.
6. Keeping a negative time or length in a word problem.
7. Multiplying by a constant and changing the sign of one term.
8. Using relations for cubic polynomials or the division algorithm (not in the 2026–27 syllabus).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a quadratic polynomial?
questions.solution_md: A polynomial has only whole-number powers of $x$. $\dfrac1x = x^{-1}$ and $\sqrt x = x^{1/2}$ are not allowed, so (a) and (c) are not polynomials. $x^3 - 1$ has degree $3$ (cubic). $3 - 2x^2$ has degree $2$: quadratic.

questions.solution_md: Solve $4x + 6 = 0$: $x = -\dfrac64 = -\dfrac32$. In general the zero of $ax + b$ is $-\dfrac ba$. Option (b) drops the sign; option (c) inverts the fraction.

questions.stem_md: The graph of a quadratic polynomial $y = p(x)$ cuts the $x$-axis only at $(-2, 0)$ and $(5, 0)$. The zeroes of $p(x)$ are
questions.solution_md: A zero is the $x$-coordinate of a point where the graph meets the $x$-axis: $-2$ and $5$. Option (a) flips the signs, which happens when students think of the factors $(x + 2)(x - 5)$ instead of the zeroes.

questions.stem_md: The maximum number of zeroes a cubic polynomial can have is
questions.solution_md: A polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ zeroes; its graph meets the $x$-axis at most $n$ times. A cubic has degree $3$, so at most $3$ zeroes.

questions.stem_md: The graph of $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ is a parabola that opens **downward**. Then
questions.solution_md: The sign of the leading coefficient decides the shape: $a > 0$ opens upward, $a < 0$ opens downward. The constant $c$ only gives the $y$-intercept, and $b$ shifts the parabola sideways.

questions.stem_md: The sum of the zeroes of $3x^2 - 5x + 2$ is
questions.solution_md: Sum $= -\dfrac ba = -\dfrac{-5}{3} = \dfrac53$. **Check:** $3x^2 - 5x + 2 = (3x - 2)(x - 1)$, zeroes $\dfrac23$ and $1$, sum $\dfrac53$. Option (b) forgets the minus sign in $-\dfrac ba$; option (c) is the product.

questions.stem_md: The product of the zeroes of $4x^2 - 9$ is
questions.solution_md: Here $a = 4$, $b = 0$, $c = -9$, so the product $= \dfrac ca = -\dfrac94$. **Check:** the zeroes are $\pm\dfrac32$ and $\dfrac32 \times \left(-\dfrac32\right) = -\dfrac94$. Option (d) is one of the zeroes.

questions.stem_md: A quadratic polynomial whose zeroes are $-3$ and $4$ is
questions.solution_md: Sum $= -3 + 4 = 1$, product $= -12$. Polynomial: $x^2 - (\text{sum})x + \text{product} = x^2 - x - 12$. **Check:** $(x + 3)(x - 4) = x^2 - x - 12$. Option (a) uses $+(\text{sum})x$.

questions.stem_md: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the zeroes of $x^2 - 6x + 4$, then $\alpha^2 + \beta^2$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\alpha + \beta = 6$ and $\alpha\beta = 4$. $\alpha^2 + \beta^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 2\alpha\beta = 36 - 8 = 28$. Option (b) forgets to subtract $2\alpha\beta$; option (c) adds it.

The zeroes of $5x^2 + 13x + k$ are reciprocals of each other. Then $k$ equals
questions.solution_md: If the zeroes are $\alpha$ and $\dfrac1\alpha$, their product is $1$. So $\dfrac k5 = 1$, giving $k = 5$. **Check:** $5x^2 + 13x + 5$ has real zeroes (since $169 > 100$) whose product is $\dfrac55 = 1$.

questions.stem_md: The zeroes of $x^2 + (k - 3)x - 16$ are equal in size but opposite in sign. Then $k$ equals
questions.solution_md: If the zeroes are $\alpha$ and $-\alpha$, their sum is $0$. Sum $= -(k - 3) = 0$, so $k = 3$. Then $x^2 - 16$ has zeroes $4$ and $-4$. Option (c) confuses $k$ with a zero.

questions.stem_md: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the zeroes of $x^2 - 5x + 6$, then $\dfrac{1}{\alpha} + \dfrac{1}{\beta}$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac1\alpha + \dfrac1\beta = \dfrac{\alpha + \beta}{\alpha\beta} = \dfrac56$. **Check:** zeroes $2$ and $3$: $\dfrac12 + \dfrac13 = \dfrac56$. Option (b) inverts the fraction.

questions.stem_md: A quadratic polynomial whose zeroes are $2 + \sqrt{3}$ and $2 - \sqrt{3}$ is
questions.solution_md: Sum $= 4$; product $= (2 + \sqrt3)(2 - \sqrt3) = 4 - 3 = 1$. Polynomial: $x^2 - 4x + 1$. Option (d) adds $4 + 3$ for the product.

questions.stem_md: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the zeroes of $x^2 + px + q$, then a polynomial whose zeroes are $2\alpha$ and $2\beta$ is
questions.solution_md: $\alpha + \beta = -p$ and $\alpha\beta = q$. New sum $= 2(\alpha + \beta) = -2p$; new product $= 4\alpha\beta = 4q$. Polynomial: $x^2 - (-2p)x + 4q = x^2 + 2px + 4q$. Option (b) doubles the product instead of multiplying it by $4$; option (d) is $2(x^2 + px + q)$, which has the **same** zeroes as before.

questions.solution_md: Zeroes are exactly the $x$-coordinates of the points where the graph meets the $x$-axis. No meeting point means no zero.

questions.stem_md: The polynomials $x^2 + 5x + 6$ and $x^2 - 5x + 6$ have the same product of zeroes.
questions.solution_md: Both have $\dfrac ca = 6$. (Zeroes $-2, -3$ and $2, 3$: products $6$ and $6$; the sums $-5$ and $5$ differ.)

questions.stem_md: There is exactly one quadratic polynomial whose zeroes are $1$ and $4$.
questions.solution_md: $k(x^2 - 5x + 4)$ has zeroes $1$ and $4$ for **every** non-zero $k$, e.g. $x^2 - 5x + 4$ and $2x^2 - 10x + 8$. There are infinitely many.

questions.stem_md: The zero of $p(x) = 5x - 3$ is ___.
questions.solution_md: $5x - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac35 = 0.6$.

questions.stem_md: The graph of a quadratic polynomial is a curve called a ___.
questions.solution_md: The graph of $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ ($a \ne 0$) is a **parabola**, opening upward if $a > 0$ and downward if $a < 0$.

questions.stem_md: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the zeroes of $2x^2 - 10x + 7$, then $\alpha + \beta =$ ___.
questions.solution_md: $\alpha + \beta = -\dfrac ba = \dfrac{10}{2} = 5$.

questions.stem_md: A quadratic polynomial whose zeroes have sum $0$ and product $-5$ is $x^2 -$ ___.
questions.solution_md: $x^2 - (\text{sum})x + \text{product} = x^2 - 0 \cdot x + (-5) = x^2 - 5$.

questions.stem_md: If $3$ is a zero of $x^2 + kx + 15$, then $k =$ ___.
questions.solution_md: $9 + 3k + 15 = 0 \Rightarrow 3k = -24 \Rightarrow k = -8$. **Check:** $x^2 - 8x + 15 = (x - 3)(x - 5)$.

questions.stem_md: Find the product of the zeroes of $6x^2 - 5x - 6$.
questions.solution_md: Product $= \dfrac ca = \dfrac{-6}{6} = -1$. **Check:** $6x^2 - 5x - 6 = (3x + 2)(2x - 3)$, zeroes $-\dfrac23$ and $\dfrac32$, product $-1$.

questions.stem_md: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the zeroes of $x^2 - 8x + 13$, find $\alpha^2 + \beta^2$.
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** $\alpha + \beta = 8$, $\alpha\beta = 13$. **Step 2.** $\alpha^2 + \beta^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 2\alpha\beta = 64 - 26 = 38$.

questions.stem_md: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the zeroes of $x^2 - 8x + 13$, find $(\alpha - \beta)^2$.
questions.solution_md: $(\alpha - \beta)^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 4\alpha\beta = 64 - 52 = 12$.

The length and breadth (in metres) of a rectangular plot in Ahmedabad are the zeroes of $x^2 - 23x + 120$. Find the length of its diagonal, in metres, **without** finding the length and breadth separately.
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** $l + b = 23$, $lb = 120$. **Step 2.** Diagonal$^2 = l^2 + b^2 = (l + b)^2 - 2lb = 529 - 240 = 289$. **Step 3.** Diagonal $= 17$ m. (Check: the sides are $15$ m and $8$ m.)

questions.stem_md: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the zeroes of $2x^2 + 7x + 3$, find $\alpha^2\beta + \alpha\beta^2$.
questions.solution_md: $\alpha^2\beta + \alpha\beta^2 = \alpha\beta(\alpha + \beta) = \dfrac32 \times \left(-\dfrac72\right) = -\dfrac{21}{4} = -5.25$.

questions.stem_md: The parabola $y = x^2 - 6x + 5$ cuts the $x$-axis at points $A$ and $B$. Find the distance $AB$.
For the polynomial $x^2 - (k + 2)x + 2k$, the sum of the zeroes equals their product. Find $k$.
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** Sum $= k + 2$, product $= 2k$. **Step 2.** $k + 2 = 2k \Rightarrow k = 2$. **Check:** $x^2 - 4x + 4 = (x - 2)^2$ has zeroes $2, 2$: sum $4$, product $4$.

questions.stem_md: A ball is thrown upward from the roof of a building in Mumbai. Its height above the ground after $t$ seconds is $h(t) = -5t^2 + 20t + 25$ metres. After how many seconds does it hit the ground?
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** The ball hits the ground when $h(t) = 0$: $-5(t^2 - 4t - 5) = -5(t - 5)(t + 1) = 0$. **Step 2.** $t = 5$ or $t = -1$; time cannot be negative, so $t = 5$ s. The zero $-1$ is rejected.

questions.stem_md: Find the zeroes of $x^2 + 2x - 15$ and verify the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients.

answer.model_answer_md:
$x^2 + 2x - 15 = x^2 + 5x - 3x - 15 = (x + 5)(x - 3)$. Zeroes: $-5$ and $3$.

Sum $= -5 + 3 = -2 = -\dfrac{2}{1} = -\dfrac ba$. Product $= -15 = \dfrac{-15}{1} = \dfrac ca$. Verified.

questions.solution_md: Split $2x$ as $5x - 3x$ (since $5 \times (-3) = -15$ and $5 - 3 = 2$).

questions.stem_md: Find a quadratic polynomial whose zeroes have sum $\dfrac{5}{2}$ and product $-\dfrac{3}{2}$. Also find its zeroes.

answer.model_answer_md:
$x^2 - \dfrac52x - \dfrac32$, or multiplying by $2$: $2x^2 - 5x - 3$.

$2x^2 - 5x - 3 = 2x^2 - 6x + x - 3 = (2x + 1)(x - 3)$, so the zeroes are $3$ and $-\dfrac12$. (Sum $\dfrac52$, product $-\dfrac32$ ✓.)

questions.solution_md: Use $k[x^2 - (\text{sum})x + \text{product}]$ with $k = 2$ to clear fractions, then factorise.

questions.stem_md: The graph of $y = p(x)$, a quadratic polynomial, is shown. (a) Write the zeroes of $p(x)$. (b) Write the value of $p(0)$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The graph meets the $x$-axis at $x = -2$ and $x = 3$, so the zeroes are $-2$ and $3$.

(b) The graph meets the $y$-axis at $6$, so $p(0) = 6$.

questions.solution_md: Zeroes are read on the $x$-axis; $p(0)$ is the $y$-intercept. (Here $p(x) = -x^2 + x + 6 = -(x + 2)(x - 3)$.)

questions.stem_md: Find the zeroes of $9t^2 - 16$ and verify the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients.

answer.model_answer_md:
$9t^2 - 16 = (3t - 4)(3t + 4)$, so the zeroes are $\dfrac43$ and $-\dfrac43$.

Sum $= 0 = -\dfrac{0}{9}$ ✓ (the coefficient of $t$ is $0$). Product $= -\dfrac{16}{9} = \dfrac ca$ ✓.

questions.stem_md: $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the zeroes of $x^2 - 3x - 10$. Find a quadratic polynomial whose zeroes are $\alpha + 1$ and $\beta + 1$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\alpha + \beta = 3$, $\alpha\beta = -10$.

New sum $= (\alpha + \beta) + 2 = 5$. New product $= \alpha\beta + (\alpha + \beta) + 1 = -10 + 3 + 1 = -6$.
